questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of business ethics?
options: The moral principles guiding how a business behaves, beyond what the law requires
The laws a business must obey in the country where it trades
The accounting standards used to prepare financial statements
The procedures set out in a business's employee handbook
questions.why: Ethics goes beyond legal compliance to what is right, so a legal decision can still be unethical.
whyNot: Law is the minimum standard; ethics asks what should be done above that.
Accounting standards govern reporting, not the wider morality of decisions.
Internal procedures are rules; ethics is the principles that should shape them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of corporate social responsibility?
options: A business voluntarily taking responsibility for its social and environmental impact
A business obeying all the laws that apply to it
A business maximising returns for its shareholders
A business paying the taxes it legally owes
questions.why: The essential word is voluntary: CSR is what the business does beyond its legal obligations.
whyNot: Legal compliance is the minimum requirement, not CSR.
That is the shareholder model of business purpose.
Paying legally owed tax is an obligation, not voluntary responsibility.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines greenwashing?
options: Presenting a business as more environmentally responsible than it actually is
Reducing packaging in order to cut costs
Investing in renewable energy for a factory
Publishing an annual environmental report
questions.why: Greenwashing is the gap between environmental claim and actual behaviour, and it is riskier than saying nothing because the gap becomes the story.
whyNot: That is a genuine cost saving that happens to help the environment.
That is real action rather than a misleading claim.
Reporting is only greenwashing if the content misrepresents what the business does.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the trade-off between profit and ethics?
options: Behaving ethically reduces profit, at least in the short term
Ethical businesses can never be profitable
Profit and ethics are always in permanent conflict
Ethical behaviour has no effect on costs
questions.why: Paying suppliers fairly, sourcing responsibly and refusing questionable business all reduce short-run profit, and acknowledging that is what makes an answer credible.
whyNot: Many ethical businesses are highly profitable, particularly over the long run.
The conflict is usually short-run; over a long horizon the two often align.
Ethical choices frequently raise costs, which is precisely the trade-off.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pay-related ethical issue named in the specification?
options: Executive pay ratios compared with median employee pay
The date on which salaries are paid each month
Whether staff are paid weekly or monthly
The currency in which staff are paid
questions.why: Large gaps between the highest and median paid raise fairness questions and affect morale, which is why pay ratios are examinable.
whyNot: Payment dates are an administrative matter rather than an ethical issue.
Payment frequency is an administrative choice, though very long gaps can create hardship.
Currency of payment is a practical matter, not an ethical one in itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest commercial argument for behaving ethically?
options: Reputational damage is expensive and slow to repair
Ethical behaviour is always cheaper in the short run
Ethical behaviour is required by law in all countries
Customers always pay more for ethical products
questions.why: Scandals can destroy revenue much faster than the cost savings that created them, and regulation usually follows public anger.
whyNot: In the short run ethical choices usually cost more, which is the trade-off.
If it were legally required it would be compliance, not ethics.
Customers often say they will pay more and then do not, which is the key gap to notice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the sharpest criticism of relying on customers to reward ethical behaviour?
options: Customers frequently say they will pay more for ethics and then do not
Customers are unaware that ethical issues exist
Customers have no legal right to choose suppliers
Ethical products cannot be advertised
questions.why: The gap between stated and actual willingness to pay is a genuinely sharp evaluation point, because it undermines the whole commercial case.
whyNot: Awareness is generally high; the problem is behaviour, not knowledge.
Customers are free to choose, which is why the claim is made in the first place.
Ethical positioning is a very common form of advertising.

questions.stem: Why can performance incentives lead to unethical behaviour?
options: You get the behaviour you reward, so short-term targets encourage the conduct that causes scandals
Incentives are always illegal
Bonuses reduce employee motivation
Incentives make employees work fewer hours
questions.why: Unethical outcomes are often the predictable result of an incentive scheme rather than of bad individuals, which is why the incentive link is worth naming.
whyNot: Performance pay is lawful and very widely used.
Bonuses generally raise effort; the problem is which behaviour they direct it towards.
Incentives typically increase effort rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a genuine cost saving that also improves environmental performance?
options: Reducing energy use, material use and waste
Publishing a sustainability report
Sponsoring a local sports team
Appointing a head of sustainability
questions.why: Using less input costs less, which is why sustainability and efficiency often point the same way and weaken the claim that ethics always costs money.
whyNot: Reporting costs money without directly reducing environmental impact.
Sponsorship is community investment with no direct environmental saving.
That is an administrative cost, useful but not itself a saving.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the triple bottom line?
options: Judging a business on its social and environmental performance as well as its financial performance
Producing three separate sets of financial statements
Reporting profit before interest, after interest and after tax
Dividing profit between shareholders, employees and the community
questions.why: People, planet and profit: three dimensions of performance rather than one.
whyNot: It is about the dimensions measured, not the number of statements produced.
Those are all financial measures of the same thing.
Distributing profit is a separate decision from how performance is judged.

questions.stem: Why can greenwashing be worse for a business than making no environmental claims at all?
options: The gap between the claim and the behaviour becomes the story
Environmental claims are illegal in most countries
It costs more than genuine environmental action
It prevents a business from advertising at all
questions.why: A business that says nothing is judged on its behaviour; one that claims more than it delivers invites a reputational attack on its honesty as well as its conduct.
whyNot: Environmental claims are lawful provided they are not misleading.
Greenwashing is usually cheaper than real action, which is why it happens.
It does not remove the ability to advertise, though it raises the risk of doing so.

questions.stem: A business argues that it must match a competitor's cost cutting even though it involves poorer supplier conditions. What is the strongest counter-argument?
options: Reputational and regulatory risk may cost more than the saving, and staff and customers notice
Cost cutting never reduces costs in practice
Competitors are legally obliged to match ethical standards
Suppliers cannot change their conditions
questions.why: The saving is certain and small; the risk is uncertain and potentially large, and regulation usually follows public anger.
whyNot: Cost cutting genuinely does reduce costs, which is why the trade-off is real.
No such obligation exists, which is why the competitive pressure arises.
Supplier conditions are exactly what is being changed in this decision.

questions.stem: In a resort business, why do environmental ethics and long-term profit align particularly closely?
options: The reef is the product, so damaging it to save money destroys the asset
Environmental spending is tax deductible
Tourists are not interested in the environment
Environmental regulation is identical in every country
questions.why: Where the natural environment is the thing customers are paying for, an environmental stance is also a commercial one.
whyNot: Tax treatment is a minor consideration next to destroying the core attraction.
Environmental quality is central to what these customers are buying.
Regulation varies widely, which is part of why ethics goes beyond law.

questions.stem: A business faces a short-run cost from improving staff accommodation on a remote site. What is the strongest long-run commercial argument for spending it?
options: Better retention, which matters most where a departing specialist cannot be replaced mid-season
It will immediately increase the price customers pay
It removes the need for any recruitment
It guarantees higher occupancy rates
questions.why: The return comes through retention, and the value of retention is highest where replacing someone quickly is impossible.
whyNot: Customers do not usually pay more because staff accommodation improved.
Some recruitment is always needed; the aim is to reduce avoidable turnover.
Occupancy depends on demand and marketing, not directly on staff accommodation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a legitimate argument for prioritising profit over an ethical stance?
options: Competitors that cut costs will undercut the business, and jobs depend on it remaining viable
Ethical behaviour is against the interests of customers
Shareholders have no legal right to returns
Unethical behaviour carries no reputational risk
questions.why: A business that prices itself out of the market helps nobody, so the competitive position is a real constraint on how far an ethical stance can go.
whyNot: Ethical behaviour usually serves customers; the constraint is cost and competition.
Shareholders do have a claim on returns, which is the basis of the argument.
Reputational risk is substantial, which is the main counter-argument.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an ethical stance?
options: The position a business takes on how it will trade, even where that reduces profit
The minimum legal standard a business must meet
The proportion of profit a business donates to charity
The percentage of suppliers a business audits each year
questions.why: An ethical stance is a chosen position on conduct that the business holds to even when it is costly.
whyNot: The legal minimum is compliance, not a stance.
Donation is one possible expression of a stance, not the stance itself.
Auditing is a monitoring activity rather than a position on conduct.
